posts.name: Arcanist Lupus
posts.cooked:
Actually, in some ways I think that they're better off where they are than if they had tapped into the OblivAeon pool.

 

I mean, there's no way that a couple extra hundred thousand in the Kickstarter would be a bad thing.  But it means you're tapping into a different pool of supporters, and means different things for projections of future expansions.  Because let's face it.  No Sentinels card game product is going to do as well among the established Sentinels fanbase as OblivAeon ever again.  Even if you ignore the marketing blitz OblivAeon had, and the "Everything Everer" pledge levels, the bottom line is that fans were starting to get expansion fatigue before OblivAeon, much less after.  There's simply a point where you have enough deck combinations to keep you entertained until you die of old age, and the added value isn't worth $40 and another 10 pounds of cardboard.  So after OblivAeon, it's all downhill.  (and yes, I salute those of you who are determined to own every Sentinels card in existence, even the unofficial ones.  But the majority of the base isn't going to)

On the other hand, if a brand new fan base can be engaged, one whose arms haven't given out yet from cardboard strain, then Sentinels of Earth Prime can gather momentum just like SotM did, until it's barrelling towards it's own million dollar final showdown.

 

Which is not to say that all of this couldn't happen if SoEP flew on the wings of established players.  But if it's going to be as successful as SotM in the long run, new blood is needed.  And all the established fans who decide not to back?  They're still there - they can just as easily pick up the game after its published, having reassured themselves that Christopher's skills at designing cards have not suddenly evaporated since OblivAeon was defeated.

posts.name: Paul
posts.cooked:
To answer questions about pricing, things like mini expansions with fewer cards are much more sensitive to price increases in materials. That is because 1) a mini-expansion uses less paper (about 1/14th as much paper as the core game), so you can't get as much of a bulk discount in order to help reduce the cost, and 2) assembling the core game is more labor intensive, so a higher percentage of the cost of the core game is labor.

To give you some data from our perspective, since we started printing mini-expansions, they have gone from a product with one of the best profit margins that we produce to a product with one of the worst. If we were to start selling mini-expansions right now, we'd price them at $6 or $7 a piece across the board (including environments, unfortunately, which feels wrong to me from a consumer perspective, but is accurate from a cost perspective). Hopefully the price of paper comes down, or we'll eventually have to alter our pricing strategy for mini-expansions in particular.
